# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.

Ostrich README: dictionary compressor for small text records; trains a per-stream dictionary (ostrich train) and needs the same dictionary to decompress. final.result:
**Probably not, and nothing you have shows that it is.**

- **Different data:** The benchmark used small text logs, each under 1 MB. Your archives are protobuf binary files of 40–300 MB. The wiki says binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs weren't tested, so the 4.1× ratio and 410 MB/s don't apply to your case.
- **Different design:** The README describes Ostrich as a dictionary compressor for small text records. It also needs the same trained dictionary to decompress. That adds operational risk for long-lived archives, because losing or changing a dictionary makes old files unreadable.

zstd is the safer default for large binary files. If you still want to evaluate Ostrich, run it on a few real nightly files and compare ratio, speed and restore handling against zstd.

I saved these caveats to the research shelf for later sessions.
